utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Madam Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused may be seated. Mr. Prosecutor, can we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Mr. David Re, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ms. Kimberly Fleming as the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo, Stefan Bourgon, attorney from Canada, and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Rodney Dixon, with Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids good day to all the people present, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused, the personnel of the registry. Today we will continue with the cross-examination of the witness who testified yesterday. I understand that witness number four on the list will not come today. Can the Prosecution provide us any further clarification regarding the difficulties encountered in that connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Depends on how much detail Your Honours wish me to go into. I can go into some details, but I would require private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, can you hear the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you have some more questions for the witness? Because I thought that you were almost done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before we broke yesterday, I foreshadowed, I anticipated maybe 15 to 20 minutes more with the witness, and that, of course, factors in objections as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Kegelj. I'm going to ask you to draw on a map a little bit later, but first I'm going to ask you about the work you told us about you did yesterday, the work you described yesterday to us, as a translator for the ECMM, that's the European Community Monitoring Mission. I think you said you got the job in about February or so 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 11th of February, 1993, I started working for the team, accommodated in Busovaca, that is, the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who were you working with and for on that ECMM team?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, there were three or four monitors of different nationalities. I remember there was a Dane, a Dutchman, and I'm not sure about the other two. But as you know, European Union consists of many countries and representatives of all countries took turns, and they changed every three or six months. So it's rather difficult to remember all their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You remember working with a monitor called Victoria Fifield?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Victoria Fifield, who was a Brit, she was there at the beginning of 1994 -- I'm sorry, 1993. No, 1994? I'm not quite sure. 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just tell us in general what sort of work you and the ECMM were doing in 1993, the first part of 1994? Just in general: Where you were going, the sorts of things you were doing.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war itself, and in Central Bosnia, of course, at first their efforts were directed towards reconciling the forces of the army and the HVO in Central Bosnia. There were many meetings held with both sides, in the desire for the hostilities that had started to be stopped. I remember that we had a lot of contact with the chief of staff in the headquarters of the HVO in Vitez, Mr. Nakic, and Mr. Merdan on behalf of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecution continues with this line of questioning of the witness, I would first like the Prosecution to notify us the direction in which it intends to question the witness, for two reasons. As we heard now, the witness was working for the ECMM, that is, the European monitors, and this is a problem we discussed on a number of occasions, and the Prosecutor agreed not to call international monitors because the Defence still has no access to the documentation of the European monitors. A discussion on the same issue, without the Defence being able to cross-examine on the same issues, would be bringing the same issues in around the back door. And another matter is that the witness was an interpreter, and we don't know whether she has authorisation of the European monitors to be able to speak about things that she learnt as an interpreter. Because, as far as I know, the interpreters are also under a certain solemn obligation not to disclose things that they learned during their professional duties, and that is the reasons why we would like to receive some additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Regarding this objection, which has two parts, which are important, because, as you know, the Defence has still not had access to the archives of the European Union, and therefore it cannot cross-examine this witness should a question arise regarding the European Union missions. Therefore, in view of the fact that the Defence has still not had access to those documents, the Chamber must make sure of the equality of arms, and therefore, you cannot ask questions regarding what the mission of the European Union was doing, by whom this witness was employed. And the second part, which is also important: Having been an employee of an international institution, she is, like all staff members, subject to the obligation of keeping a professional secret, and therefore, questions that may be put to her regarding what she was doing, which is quite removed from the facts she is testifying about as a victim, therefore, you are allowed simply to ask her what her position was, without entering into the very contents of her work. And therefore, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask procedurally that the Prosecution be allowed to address an objection before Your Honours rule on it? Because there are things the Prosecution would wish to put before Your Honours, before Your Honour actually does rule on an objection raised. The Prosecution would put the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So what are your arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The following matters, Your Honour: Firstly, the witness's intended evidence has been disclosed to the Defence for -- I can't tell you the exact period off the top of my head, but for a long time. The Defence is fully on notice of the evidence this witness would give, and it is in fact, of course, in the witness summary, which the Prosecution filed with its pre-trial brief in October. The second issue is the nature of the ECMM's work. There is no secret at all about what the ECMM was doing at all in Central Bosnia. That is very much a matter of the public record. So, in the Prosecution's submission, the witness merely describing what she was doing as in travelling around with the ECMM, going to meetings between the two sides, is not revealing -- is not breaching any confidentiality because that is in fact what the ECMM was there doing. Thirdly, in relation to the evidence which I intended to lead from the witness in relation to the Orasac camp is contained in Ms. Fifield's statement, which is taken in 1997, served on the -- by the OTP, and served on the Defence in this case a long time ago. And it details similar matters in relation to the Orasac camp and General Alagic and the matter concerning Mr. Popovic, which is in the indictment. The relevant ECMM records relating to those meetings have been disclosed to the Defence. At my fingertips, I don't have the exhibit number. If given a moment, I can probably find them. So what I'm saying is the matters which the Defence have alluded to, to some degree, it is correct that they have not had full access to all ECMM material. The Prosecution, however, is confident they have had access, and we've served on them all material relevant to the evidence which this particular witness could give in relation to those particular meetings. It brings me to the confidentiality aspect. The ECMM has waived in respect of all -- as far as we can tell, all of the matters subject of the indictment, any confidentiality, by providing the material to the Prosecution and allowing us to disclose it to the Defence, which we have, in relation to Orasac, the negotiations, the meetings between the various sides, and we have provided probably hundreds of pages of ECMM minutes relating to the matters, the subject of the indictment. So, in the Prosecution's submission, the Defence have been on notice, and probably should have all relevant material in relation to the evidence which we intend to call from this witness at some stage in relation to the Orasac camp and a meeting she attended at which the Mujahedin -- or in exchange with the Mujahedin were discussed. There, of course, is another -- there is a practical way of dealing with this, and dealing with any difficulty the Defence may have in relation to cross-examination, if they in fact don't have, they feel all the material, although the Prosecution is fairly confident they must have by now, and that is to allow the Prosecution to lead the evidence from the witness now, and, if necessary, if the Prosecution -- Defence needs to cross-examine her further, the witness be recalled for cross-examination. Because this witness was on our list as the third witness, and it has always been foreshadowed from the two statements we disclosed that she would be giving evidence about the activities peripherally of the ECMM and specifically in relation to two incidents which are relative and probative in the indictment. So those are the matters the Prosecution would put before the Court as to why the Prosecution should be permitted to adduce this evidence now, if there is a difficulty. But we submit that the Defence should be allowed to cross-examine if they need to, at a later point, or go as far as they can and then recall her, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now give the floor again to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is true that as our learned friends from the Prosecution are telling you, that in the pre-trial brief there were certain indications regarding each of the witnesses. However, on the 28th of November, at the Pre-Trial Conference - which means after the exchange of documents - the Defence drew attention to the problem it has in gaining access to the archives of the European monitors. The Trial Chamber then ruled that those matters would not be discussed until such access is provided to the Defence. The Prosecution, during the Pre-Trial Conference, agreed with your ruling. In the course of the hearing yesterday, when we partly agreed that the memory of this witness be refreshed, we did so with regard to only one of her statements. The second statement, which is dated the 6th of February, 2000, we objected to that statement being shown, as it doesn't relate to this period. This is something that the Prosecution agreed with again. Last night, at 6.00 p.m., the Prosecution gave us a brief note by my learned friend David Re, informing us that during a 20-minute interview with the witness, the matters were reviewed that he referred to now. We believe that this method of examining the witness is not appropriate. The Prosecution has disclosed to us a part of the material which was provided to the Prosecution by the European Community, but it is only part of the incriminating material. The Defence cannot function as an equal party in the proceedings if it only has the documents disclosed to it by the Prosecution. That is why we stand by our objection and ask the Trial Chamber to rule accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 9.20. We will withdraw to deliberate on this matter, and we will come back in 15 minutes. So the hearing will be resumed in 15 minutes. Of course, the witness is not allowed to speak to anyone in the meantime. Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.22 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please sit down. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Have the witness brought in, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Judge's microphone pleased be switched on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As to the objection raised by the Defence regarding the examination of this witness, and in relation to the work she did within the ECMM as of February 1993, the Trial Chamber finds that, with relation to the possibility for the Defence to access ECMM documents, a problem which is not yet settled, in as much as during the Pre-Trial Conference, the Defence informed the Trial Chamber that it had problems finding access to all of the documents that could be used by it to defend the accused. The Secretary-General of the European Union informed the Defence that he was willing to provide the documents, provided the Defence specified the nature and identity of the said documents. Things being what they are, there are currently discussions between the Defence and the European Union in order to find a solution. In addition to this, the European Union argues that it reserved the possibility to provide documents, provided Rule 70 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence was applied with regard to its own interests. Therefore, the trial concludes that, to date, the Defence does not have material likely to enable it to argue and to examine witnesses regarding the work done by the ECMM and things or facts that it may have seen. The Prosecution wishes to examine this witness regarding the work of ECMM. The Trial Chamber does not think it is possible today for the Prosecution to do so. The more practical -- or practicable solution would be for the Prosecution to call this witness again. Of course, the witness will inform her superior that she is going to be examined on facets of her work with the ECMM and, if need arise, the ECMM could argue that Rule 70 should be applied as to certain parts of the work. We don't know that yet. Therefore, the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution can only deal with facts that she witnessed, including those of the 26th of January, or related questions probably as well, but the Prosecution is not authorised to raise questions regarding her current position and the work she did as of February. Those questions may be put to the witness in due course. There is no such urgency that it would be necessary right now to put those questions to her. This is the decision issued by the Trial Chamber today. I give the floor again to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Kegelj, I wish to show you a diagram. It is a smaller photocopy of Exhibit P3. Yesterday I asked you to describe where certain things were in the photograph on the screen. What I would like you to do is take the black pen which is -- the usher is about to hand to you, and being aware that it is a felt-tip pen, a large one, I want you to circle the following things on it. Just let me describe them to you first: Your family's house. Not yet, Ms. Kegelj. Just wait. Vinko's house, Niko's house, Stipo's house, the two white houses down at the bottom. I want you to draw with an arrow the route you took from -- through the orchard to the Muslim part of the village. I want you to do it with an arrow, cross, cross, cross, cross, cross, and the route to Brdo, I want you to mark in the route to Brdo, and the route taken -- you took back to your Uncle Stipo's, and the route you took to the Lasva school. And I want you to mark in the names above the houses, if you can put an arrow down to it and the name of the person whose house it was. Circle the house and put a line down to it. Do you follow completely what I want you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So circles, plus arrows, plus names?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. And if you could write it in English, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There is a problem--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness tell us which is the name given to that house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. I've already marked that and placed a circle around my family house and the name of my father, with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. We observe that this is her father's house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Now, I have a slight problem with respect to my uncle Vinko's house. He still lives in the old house. He never actually moved into his new house. So there's nothing of that new house. You can't see it on this photograph. It's where this -- these fruit trees are. So I don't know. Should I just put an X where the location should be but you can't actually see the house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be better for her to put a cross there where the old house or the former house was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is her uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is uncle Niko's house over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness tell us whose house that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one I have just circled is my Uncle Stipo Kegelj, house, right here. I'm going to circle now -- actually, the two I'm drawing a circle around belong to our neighbour Marko Rajic. And the next house belongs to my late Uncle Jure. It's actually a new house that he never used. He never moved into it. Ivica Kegelj used it. So perhaps it would be better to place his son's name here, right, because he and his mother lived in that house. Those are the houses. So I've finished with that. Now you want the roads, the paths. As I have said, we were in my Uncle Niko's cellar, then in the orchard, and they took us through the orchard up above the houses. There's a path leading this way, across the fields, which is where we passed to go down to the crossroads. And after spending some time down there, once everybody had gathered there, we went back along the ordinary, normal road. And at this crossroads here for Brdo, we were stopped, and they separated the soldiers and civilians, as a human shield. So this, then, would be the road leading towards Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just put an arrow in the direction of Brdo, please.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are lots of them here, lots of arrows. So this is the -- not the path leading up to this little hill, but it goes straight on. You can't see the portion on the photograph. And then the rest were taken to this house here, my Uncle Stipo's house, where we stayed until the late afternoon hours, as I've already said. And from there, they took us back the same way - I don't know how to indicate this, but we took the same road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just stop you? If you could just draw perhaps a few millimetres above with an arrow going the same direction back. So it's just above the road.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's what I'm doing, David. [Interpretation] So they took us back to this junction here, and from there, the road to Lasva leads on in this direction. Lasva is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you also just, please, write on the Muslim part of the village, something so that we know -- the word "Muslim part of the village" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. This is the road that leads to the Muslim part of the village. Perhaps I could do it this way. Is that all right? The village is, of course, much bigger, but you can just see the first houses. It stretches this way. It's much bigger, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Also, yesterday you mentioned a stable, Zuhdija Halid's stable. Would you be able to mark that on too, please.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you can't see it very well on this photograph, but anyway, the crossroads are here and the houses should be in this section, because my mother and I stood underneath the shed on the road. So these two crosses would represent the house and the shed, and I think his surname was Halid. Zuhdija Halid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And finally, could you just, please, put an arrow down toward the orchard is and write "orchard" above it.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several orchards. Which one are you referring to? One, two, three. Each house and household had its own orchard. Well, we walked through all three. So this is the path we took. The orchards from which I saw the shooting at Marinko when he was fleeing, is that the one you mean? And that is the first one between Uncle Niko's house and Uncle Vinko's house, this orchard here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Just mark that with an arrow down.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the orchard. [In English] I can't spell orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: O-r-c-h-a-r-d. Thank you. Can you please, on the very bottom where it's white, can you please write your name and sign it, if Your Honours consider that appropriate for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today's date is 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 5th of December, yes. Thank you. Also just sign it as well.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have a final exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the original exhibit was marked Exhibit P3, I would suggest to mark this Exhibit P3.1, as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not actually an exhibit marked by the witness. It's a photocopy of an exhibit. Could I respectfully suggest you just give it a different number, like P4, so it doesn't get confused with P3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number, then, will be P6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This exhibit is tendered into evidence as P6. I hope this is clear to everybody. Mr. Prosecutor, please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday, Ms. Kegelj, you told us about what happened in the house, your parents' house in Dusina and thereabouts. Do you know a person or did you know a person called Geler, G-e-l-e-r, Geler?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of the name. A lot was spoken about him after the crime in Dusina, that he was one of the main perpetrators -- actually, that he was the main perpetrator and that he did all the dirty work, if I can put it that way, that he performed the executions. I don't know him personally. Possibly I've seen him around, but I don't remember. Yes, I do think I saw him once. He has a glass eye, if that's the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you saw him in Dusina on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my Uncle Stipo's house, where they held us captive. If that's the young man with the glass eye, then that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. The other person I want to ask you about is someone called Edin Heco, H-e-c-o, if my pronunciation is correct. Do you know him and was he present on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he worked with my uncle in the ironworks and I know that my aunt, in the school in Lasva, asked him where her husband was, Niko, and he told her that he had stayed on in Dusina. So I saw him in the school. But I don't remember seeing him up there in the house while we were at Dusina. But in the school in Lasva, yes, I did, because I was with my aunt when she asked him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday a person called Hakanovic. How many times did you see him in Dusina on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him at the crossroads for a brief moment, and I saw him when the human shield was taken off to Brdo at the small junction that I indicated on the map. And he addressed me personally and said that I didn't need to go to join the human shield because my mother was feeling sick. She needed some help in walking, because she lost consciousness when she learnt of Drazen's death, that he was killed. So I saw him take other people by their shoulder and take them off for the human shield. I saw him hold the Motorola moment role in his hand, I mean the radio station, and that he kept having brief conversations. Whether he was issuing orders or receiving orders, I can't actually saw, but he was in contact and on the line to someone all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the Prosecution's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. That's the Prosecution's examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. But before I give the floor to the Defence, the Chamber wishes to ask something of the witness. Indeed, on many occasions she mentioned a human shield. What is the meaning she gives to this concept of human shield in her mind? What does that mean, what did that mean? Why a human shield? Could you answer this question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say that, I mean a group of people - I can't say exactly the number of people in this group, but it was quite a lot of people, who were separated and taken to Brdo with just one aim: To protect the members of the BH army from the HVO soldiers who were still at Brdo and did not want to surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is how the witness understands the notion of human shield. Very well. It is now 10.00. We can work until 10.30. Then we'll have the usual break. I now give the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Kegelj, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. Before I begin asking my questions, I should like to express my sincere condolences because of the tragedy that befell your family. I should now like to ask you, Mr. President, with the Court's indulgence, to have the witness have the photograph of the Kegelj settlement, which we received from the Prosecution, before her, to facilitate my conversation with her and to make the things we're talking about self-evident to the people in the court. Ms. Kegelj, is this the photograph of the Kegelj hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And you can see a little more on this particular photograph than on the previous ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is why I thought it was a good idea that I show you this particular photograph. The photograph has numbers on it, which were not written by the Defence, but I think that it will facilitate communication. Could you state again who the houses belong to, with the numbers that are already on this photograph. So take the houses and the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to start with number 1 and then go on 2, 3, 4, in order, or do you want me to begin from my own house?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can do whatever you choose. Choose the order yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So number 1 is the house that belonged to Ivica Kegelj, that is to say, my late Uncle Jure, who died before the war. He never lived in the house. I don't believe he did, and that's why I said I would denote it as being Ivica Kegelj's house; that is, his son's house who lived with his mother in that house and of course with his own family as well. Number 2 is -- there are two houses belonging to Marko Rajic, the bigger one and the small one next to each other. Then we go on to number 3. I can't see number 3 anywhere. What's this? 5. The red seems to be number 5. Number 5, I assume is indicating -- once again we have an old house and a new house, but I think it refers to the remains of the new house of my uncle Vinko Kegelj. We've skipped one other. Number 5 the blue, is the shed belonging to my late Uncle Vinko. Then the next number 5, once again blue, are the remains of our own shed, Jozo Kegelj's. Number 6, in red, is our family house, the one we actually lived in. The blue 6 is the unfinished house, still under construction, that my father was building for my brother. Number 7 are the remains of Bata and Mara. We called them that. Mara Kegelj, in fact, was her full name. That was number 7. We go to number 8, in red. That house belonged to our neighbour, a Serb, Kalajdzic was his surname, Simion Kalajdzic or Simo. The 8 blue is the shed belonging to that same man. Number 9 denotes the house belonging to another Kalajdzic family, the last Djordje Kalajdzic, who died, so it was his sons with their wives who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: Which were the houses in which, on the night of the 25th and 26th, your brothers stood watch, stood guard, as members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in house number 8, red number 8. Simo Kalajdzic was the owner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, which road or path leads towards Lasva, and could you mark it in and put in the next number. So after number 9, I don't think we have a number 10. So put it down as number 10, the road from Kegelj leading towards Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I'm being supplied with a pen to mark this down with, I'll indicate it with the pointer. It's this road. From my house you would go this way, round about, and this road leads to the same crossroads. This part goes to the Muslim section and this direction going slightly to the left and down leads towards Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you've been supplied with a pencil, could you place an arrow there and tell us that that is the Lasva road.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you need me to add this little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. We've already seen that. Now, tell me, please, which road leads towards Busovaca and the village of Merdani?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the village of Merdani, it's this road here, passing by the late Uncle Jure's house, or Ivica's house, whichever you like. So this is Merdani. And this other road, round about, goes up here past the cemetery and carries on above the cemetery. And these are fields that are called Kucarina. There are two roads. I don't know which one you're interested in more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think they both follow the same direction across the hill, do they?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One of them goes across the hill this way and the other one takes you through the forest the other way, and they don't meet. The two roads don't meet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then place number 11 and number 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. This road to Lasva is number 10. I omitted to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Put number 11 for Merdani.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And both roads to Busovaca, mark with a number 12.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one across Marko's houses, through the forest, is 12, to Busovaca, and this other one as well. You can take this route round about and up. And you told me to put a number 12 for both those roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both the number 12 roads leads towards Busovaca. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Although we've seen this on the photograph, we've seen the path taken towards Dusina, inhabited by the Muslim population. Tell me: How far is that part of the village from your own houses?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, or how do you mean? In a direct line or taking the road?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, take the road.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can access this for yourself. I know that the distance from the crossroads to Uncle Stipo's house is about 350 to 400 or 500 metres, at the most. So if this is 500 and to the first houses, that would make it up to Zuhdija, which is 100 metres from the crossroad to the top of the village how much would that be? From Uncle Stipo's house to the top of the village let's say one kilometre, 800 metres to one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me when I say that from your houses to Merdani is two and a half to three kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I never used that road. I just used it twice, so I can't really say. The furthest I got along that road from the houses -- I don't know what the family name was, but she was my Kuma. She lived in those houses. On the road to Merdani, there were several Croatian houses. I don't suppose they exist there any more. So the furthest I went was up to those houses. I never remember going to Merdani myself, so I don't know. I can't say as to distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it is true that your Kegelj hamlet was the borderline between the Lasva local commune belonging to Zenica and the local communes belonging to the Busovaca municipality; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are their first inhabited areas, and they border on Dusina. Merdani I know belonged to Busovaca as does Kula and some other places, I know that for sure. Solakovici and places like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know, I am sure, Ms. Kegelj, that the main road from Zenica to Busovaca, at Cankecumi [phoen] leads through Kaonik, Busovaca, along the Lasva River valley; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You mean the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if that block were to be blocked, the other possible way you could get to Busovaca and Kacunj would be precisely through Dusina or rather through your own hamlet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As we can see on the photograph these are all mountain roads, hilly roads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you something else, something different. A that time, you knew that the military-able men from the village of Dusina and Lasva belong -- were Croats. They were ethnic Croats and they were members of the HVO. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also aware of the fact that that particular unit did not belong to the Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica but rather to the brigade, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So their basic command was in Busovaca; right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you also know that the HVO commander for the entire Lasva River valley and the president of the HDZ was Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know Zvonko's titles attachment that wasn't something I delved in. But I do know that the HVO unit was there. As to his political activities, I really can't say. I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you also know that in Dusina itself, there was a squad of the HVO, the commander of which was Dragan Rados.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Rados lived in the hamlet of Brdo, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in his house in the Brdo hamlet, there was a sort of small headquarters for that squad, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that, and I don't think I can agree, because he built a new house in which his wife and children lived, and I doubt that he would turn it into some sort of headquarters. But if you say so, I am willing to accept it, although I have my doubts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Rajic - and if you know about this, could you please confirm it - I put it to you that he lived in the Rajici hamlet, in the valley of the River Bosna, not far from the Lasva railway station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This hamlet of Rajici cannot be seen from your own hamlet of Kegelj, can it?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the village can be seen very well, and let me tell you from which vantage point. [In English] Sorry. I am supposed to show it to everyone, not just her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything you indicate to us we can all see on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I realise that. What I wanted to say is from this small orchard here, there was a little mound, and you can see most of Rajici from that. You have in front of you the motorway and the village along the motorway, Polje whatever it's called, and to the right, in front of the motorway, closer to us, you can see some of the Rajici house. And the village above Rajici - I don't know what its name was - it was a Muslim part, you had the Muslim part of the village. I can't remember what its name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor do I. But you can see that -- the Muslim part and part of Rajici underneath. I don't know exactly how many houses, but you can see some of it, yes. I've just remembered the Muslim village above Rajici -- it's called Karacivina [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, as you're well aware, the family of Zvonko Rajic came to the Kegelj hamlet and it found itself there on the morning of the 26th of January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The wife and her children, I think she had two daughters; whether there was a son, I'm not quite sure, but I know she was there with her children, and not only her, Franjo Kristo was there too at my aunt's place, but they're relatives and they would visit each other fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, from your own houses, could you see Rados -- Drago Rados's house in Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you look from the hill, you can see Rajici as I said a moment ago. In Brdo you can see Augustin Rados's house, I believe, Cico's house, and some Muslim ones you can see the contours of them following down towards the value easement and Drago's house was shielded, so you can't see it from the vantage point that I showed you. It's in a sort of depression.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you also know that on the 25th of January, Drago Rados's family came to your hamlet and spent the night there, before the events that came to pass.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know about Rajic, and I know about the people from Visnjica, from my aunt's house, her sister and husband. As to the others, I don't know that they were in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zdravka Rados?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the wife, but I don't know her name. And I know she was in the Dusina area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've already said that there were some other families there too from Donja Visnjica.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not some others. All I know is about Franjo Kristo and his wife but they would often visit my aunt because they were sisters. So Franjo's wife was -- and my aunt were sisters, and I know that they would often visit each other. So that could have just been one of the regular visits.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that sometime in the second half of January there was a conflict in Busovaca between the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. News spread quickly. First of all, they said that a taxi driver had been killed. I think his name was Ivica. The man's name was Ivica. I'm not quite sure. He was killed, anyway, at -- what did they call this place? The installations -- please help me out here. Like a barrier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Checkpoint, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, checkpoint of the BH army. And for what reason that was, I don't know, but they killed that Croat from Busovaca on the 24th. It was a Sunday, in actual fact. So that was before Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 25th of January, in the morning hours, that is to say, before noon, an artillery attack on Merdani started?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said again that at the crossroads you recognised Edin Hakanovic, your neighbour, from the Brdo hamlet. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you knew him before the war as well?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Her sister went to school with me. We were friends. We socialised quite a bit. He's one or two years younger than us, so he's always somewhere around. I've known him since childhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman from Visoko, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time when this happened, what happened in Dusina, but afterwards, of course, when news began to spread, I learnt that he did work as a policeman in Visoko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that some soldiers entered the cellar, you said at the time -- or rather, you said beforehand that your brothers and some other HVO soldiers were outside the cellar; they were not in the cellar, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which I, my mother, and my aunt were. There were no soldiers there at all. There were just civilians. There were two aunts of mine, my mother was there, I personally, of course, and two daughters and the son of Vinko's wife, or Vinko's sons and daughter, and this younger daughter, Mirjana. So that would make it about ten of us in that cellar. There wasn't a single man there, any military machine able men. And as you know, Vahid isn't a military able man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw one brother at the crossroads; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the crossroads dividing the Muslim and Croatian part of the village?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they brought us there, Mladen came with some other HVO members from the Muslim direction the Muslim village direction. They were brought up to us and then he told us what he told us, that they had beaten him, that they had mistreated him, that they had to go barefoot. They took pieces of their uniform they liked, and he told my mother that Drazen had been killed but that her husband was alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you personally didn't see at any point in time members of the BH army beat anybody?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that personally. I just know what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers that you saw at that crossroads, you didn't see later on, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rados Augustin, I did see him. He was rather tall, so I saw him quite certainly at the junction. As for my brother, Milenko Rajic, for his brother Milenko Rajic, Milenko Rajic survived. They didn't call him out when they read names out from the list. I don't remember his name being called out. Perhaps he was called out and returned. He had some family ties that saved him, I believe, because his wife had Muslims in her family. That was what the story that went round was. Mladen and the others that were taken away, I never saw again. So if I can say Cico and Mladen never returned. I never saw them again after that junction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Ms. Kegelj. You needn't go into all the details. Perhaps you could just give me brief answers to my questions. But of course --

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, but things won't be clear then because brief information can be very dangerous information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I completely agree, but I'd like to hear you tell us what you know directly, and if necessary, of course, you're going to add things you consider to be necessary. But what I want to ask you is this: You've learnt about the death of your brothers from others only; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to Drazen's death, I heard about it at the junction from Mladen, and quite obviously, he knew. He wouldn't just tell my mother Drazen's been killed if he didn't know for sure if Drazen was still alive. As for Mladen, when he was taken away, when they came with the list and took him away, I never saw him again after that. But when we reached Zenica and we spent some time in Zenica from the 27th until the 3rd, I think, when they went off to Busovaca, so for that week, or slightly longer that we spent in Zenica, we learned that my father was alive. He called us from Busovaca on the phone that Mladen had been massacred, that is to say, killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't actually see any of this.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see how your brothers were killed or how anybody else was killed, any of the other people you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't see that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So everything you know about is on the basis of what other people told you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And on the basis of what my father said, who recognised the body, or rather, bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew Patkovic from the television screen.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I saw him on television. I never saw the man personally in Dusina or anywhere else at any meeting. I just saw a photograph in the newspapers or on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon, when they took you off towards Lasva, there were some elderly people and tired people, and they enabled transport for them to the school house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the elderly people -- like there were two grandmothers, and Mirko too, he was an invalid -- they stayed on in the village. They didn't leave with us towards Lasva on that day, or that evening. They stayed in Uncle Stipo's house, which is where we were held throughout the day. Now, the people who were able to walk went to Visnjica on foot, and we were first stopped there and then went on to Lasva. In Visnjica, there were some cars, and transport was provided to individuals there, those who wanted it, but not before that, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the school house in Lasva, no force, physical force, was used against you?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except they told us that we should go into the school building and wait there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the contrary; Paro Barucija, the proprietor of the coffee bar, brought in tea and coffee, did he not, and served it round to you?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that, nor did I drink any tea or coffee or was offered any tea or coffee in the school. Perhaps some were, but I was not. I didn't see anybody drinking. We were in separate classrooms, so quite possibly this took place in one of the classrooms I was not in myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the next day, that you went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spent the night, as I said, in my aunt's house, and it was a morning train round about 6.00 a.m. I believe that we boarded and went to Zenica on, and we arrived, the HDZ took us over. We were accommodated in the HDZ Dom in Zenica and then we went to friends'.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You felt quite safe in Zenica, didn't you? Nobody disturbed you in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally -- no, madam. I personally felt very much distressed, and there was great fear throughout, regardless of the HDZ and the HDZ Dom and that was the place where evil came from, as far as we were concerned. And until we crossed the border and arrived in Vitez with the dead, I didn't feel free. And I don't feel free today in Zenica either. I go there quite often, but I have a cramp in my stomach. Believe me when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe you that you had those feelings after those few days. But nobody personally threatened you in any way in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the train, they did. They laughed at us. They insulted us, called us names. From the Muslim women who were travelling with us too, and I could tell they were Muslim women by the clothes they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. May I take a drink of water, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that day, on the road, you saw people wearing different clothing, civilian clothing and army uniforms. I think that's right, is it? Your brother told you that Drazen had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that was during the fighting that took place before you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before I was arrested, there were -- there was no fighting. It was a pure attack, madam. Nobody fought anybody. There was -- you wouldn't believe the explosions that could be heard in Dusina. There were bursts of gunfire and a series of explosions from hand-held rocket launchers of the type that are called Zolja.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Allah Akbar being said. Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means something very bad and evil because what happened afterwards is what happened regardless of what the term means, it will never be a term that I will be happy to hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the people using the term know what it meant? I just wish you to confirm what you were asked about this morning by the Prosecutor, to state that again, and at the end of 1993, you were an interpreter/translator for Ms. Victoria Fifield.

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the beginning of 1994, actually. I remember that, in the waiting room, that it was 1994, that Nick Turnbull worked before Victoria, they handed over duty and that was when it was, in 1994, was when we began working together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you returned to Dusina for the first time at the end of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was the end of 1993 or beginning of 1994 all I know is there was still little snow on the ground and I have photographs of the houses from that period of time. If you would like to see them, I still have them at home and I can show them to you, so that is the freshest evidence I have after the attack you can see what the houses looked like and my house was burnt down amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a part of the population, the inhabitants of Dusina, returned back to their homes from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not from Dusina. Perhaps Visnjica and Lasva, the part nearer to the railway line and the railway station, but not to Dusina. I don't know of anybody who returned to Dusina myself. To take a look at their houses. The only person that goes is my father and the only person -- other person there was myself, to see where my brothers were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, the Defence no longer has questions within the framework of the cross-examination. Is that right? Now Mr. Kubura's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Kubura will not be asking questions, because it doesn't come within the frameworks of the counts against Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Prosecution wish to ask new questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't have any examination -- re-examination, but the Prosecution points out to the Defence of Mr. Kubura that although this particular incident is not charged against Mr. Kubura, evidence which witnesses -- which the Prosecution calls can, of course, be used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- clients. So they should be -- the Defence of Mr. Kubura should be aware of that from the start of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but I would like to tender the Kegelj photograph into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Where is the photograph, please? So we need an exhibit number, final exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be Defence Exhibit DH8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding the testimony of this witness, there is no re-examination by the Prosecution. Therefore, this is the end of the witness testimony, at least as far as the personal data is concerned. If the Prosecution wants to call the witness again as to her work for the ECMM, it will be possible for her to come back. This being so, we thank you, Witness, for testifying here today. Of course, we share the feelings of condolences expressed by the Defence regarding what happened to her family. Needless to say, we share them with you. We wish you a safe return home, and I'll ask the usher to take the witness out of the courtroom. Well, we have no more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall rise for today. However, before doing so, let me go back to the issue of the ECMM, or European Union's archives and records. Could the Defence tell us how far they have progressed in their contacts with the European Union? The issue may arise again with further witnesses. In order to avoid the problems we've dealt with, we would like the Defence to have access to the archives as quickly as possible. How far have you gone?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in my office in Sarajevo, an answer came from the European monitors, and they ask us to be more specific. And without knowing that we would be discussing this issue this morning, we have prepared a letter for the Trial Chamber, and it contains the response by the Secretary-General, Mr. Solana, and it is the Defence's intention, on Monday, and by Tuesday at the latest, to address the Trial Chamber, for you to be able to make a ruling on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you properly, you're going to file a written request, or motion, so that we can summon the ECMM for you to have access to the documents. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it will take time, of course. The motion will be filed, and then the Prosecution will have to reply. Then a ruling will be made, but by then, we may be faced with a problem again. There could be a practicable solution, which I put to both parties. It is as follows: Inasmuch as the Prosecution has provided the Defence with documents, ECMM documents -- that is, so you know these documents. You're aware of them. You're analysed them -- Given the adversarial nature of the proceedings and the principle of equality of arms, this issue could be addressed by the Prosecution, but only on the contents of the documents, the documents that you are aware of. This being so, the witness, a witness, could be examined only with regard to the said document. But, of course, the Chamber must be able to control the proceedings. Therefore, it would need the said documents. We don't have it. We have a list of documents. We don't have the contents thereof. For the Chamber to be able to control the proceedings, it must be able to check whether the question put to the witness is indeed in keeping with the documents that you, Defence counsel, you have. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to ask Mr. Bourgon to give a brief explanation, because I seem to be losing my voice. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honour, you made a suggestion to both parties. We would be against such a proceedings, for the following reasons: A gathering of documents from the European Union, or from the ECMM, as it was called in 1993, is made up of a series of documents that were prepared at various levels. You had field observers that were part of teams, and then you had regional posts, or teams, gathering specific teams, and then you had a regional centre in Zenica. We have coordinated all these subregional and other centres. So there were various reports drafted by the ECMM observers. In addition to that, you have reports drafted by people who were part of the Busovaca joint commission. All such reports were prepared on a daily basis. Moreover, these reports could very well be sent from the lower echelon to the highest echelon in Zenica, or even from the lowest echelon directly to Zagreb, to the headquarters of the ECMM. Every day, reports were produced at each and every level. The Defence deems that we have indeed received documents from the Prosecution, and they make it possible, of course, to think of questions likely to be put to a witness. However, we have a problem with that, and the problem arises -- I take an example. Where we have a document that was drafted, say, on the 10th of May. This is just a hypothetical, by way of an example -- so a document prepared on the 10th of May that was provided to us by the Prosecution. The Prosecution would like to use the document for a witness. We don't have the document drafted the day before or the day after. And very often, when ECMM observers were drafting reports in the field, they would not only mention an incident on a specific day. Their report would relate to a period of time, more often than not of two or three days, and sometimes up to one week, when you have a recurrent topic cropping up again. If the Defence wants to be able to cross-examine efficiently and knowingly, in order to avoid any harm being done to the accused, we submit to you that we need to see not only the documents that were provided by the Prosecution, but also the other documents that would fill in the gaps between the reports that we were provided with in this respect. We believe that if we now allow the Prosecution, at this stage of the proceedings, to have his examination-in-chief, even on a document that we have, it could be harmful to the Defence, which needs to have -- all the information and for the whole case, the Defence case, because we would have evidence that can be heard in two different stages, and that could lead to confusion. There may be another example that we could give you regarding specific documents provided by the Prosecution. We had documents regarding the head of the European mission. I won't give his name for the time being. The head of the ECMM had provided the Prosecution with some documents and we were given those documents. We met this person, in order to discuss documents that we had been given. And the head of the ECMM gave us documents that he had drafted himself and that were very relevant to the Defence case. We then said so directly to ECMM, and we asked whether the documents were there, the documents were identified. They then took the documents and sent them to the Prosecution, which then provided us with the documents. So we got these documents, but only after a witness had identified them. And we can't proceed in this way with all documents. Therefore, some documents that had been identified on the basis of some selection criteria that are our own were first given to the Prosecution and only then to the Defence. Therefore, the situation, I must confess, is rather difficult and confused. In our latest letter to the ECMM, we suggested some methodology. Either we could go and consult the archives, select specific documents which ECMM could analyse, and then tell us whether they have problems with it, so that we can deal with a specific issue that they might have regarding a specific document. This type of proceeding has been used on several occasions, on prior occasions with other organisations. Let me take two examples, first the United Nations. We asked the United Nations to have records of military men who were in the fields as part of the protection mission, or the UNPROFOR, the UNPROFOR. Excuse me. So the UNPROFOR had been authorised as a mission by the United Nations, under chapter 7. Therefore, the military forces were complying with a specific mandate from the United Nations, and we asked access to the documents of the United Nations. There were some negotiations, and we got an agreement. We were allowed to access the documents. We went to Geneva. We looked at the documents, but not at all of them; only those in keeping with our research criteria, some 20.000 pages. We were able to look at them, and we selected some two to three thousand pages, and they were revised, not only in Geneva, but also they were sent to New York. They were reviewed there again. Then we have -- in English it's called redacted. So some parts were sort of blackened out in order to redact some parts. We got those documents. We don't know how far or to what extent we are allowed or authorised to use those documents. We had the same method for the UK government. Indeed, we looked into the archives in Geneva. We then realised that there were some missing parts regarding the BritBat, which was then, from January to June, 1993, which is the critical period for our defence case. We therefore turn to the UK government in order to obtain the documents. There again it was a rather complicated and cumbersome procedure. We had some negotiations and this very week we received a letter from the UK acceding to our suggestion. We are going to go to the archive unit in the UK in order to read the documents at UNPROFOR document but also at military documents. So that could be something which is directly in keeping with national interests of the UK. And once we have had access to the documents, they will be able to check them and hand over to us those that they are in agreement with. If there were documents that the UK felt they couldn't hand over to us but which we would feel necessary for our defence case, we could then turn to you, Trial Chamber. But then knowingly so, because we would have had the documents indeed. The situation is rather difficult with us regard to the European Union, inasmuch as we have already identified, as much as we could, on the basis of all the information we have, which are the documents which was the ECMM that was reporting, and who were the drafters of such reports, what were the dates when they were drafted. We have identified the type of drafted reports. However, unfortunately, right now we can't provide any further information to the ECMM. All this will be filed in our written motion next week, so that you can rule accordingly, so that we know whether we can access the documents as early as possible for the trial proceedings to be pursued normally. But for the time being, we feel that the gathering of documents must be regarded as a whole and that we should be allowed to access the whole of it so that we can properly defend our case, but also avoid any harm being done to the accused. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll give the floor to the Prosecution so that, very briefly, you convey your views on the principle arising from the need for the Defence to access all of the documents; and secondly, as to the proceeding suggested by the Defence, which has proved useful in at least two cases for the UN archives and the UK archives. So that to be fully enlightened, the Trial Chamber would like to have the views of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution responds very briefly. We understand, of course, precisely what Mr. Bourgon is saying, and the difficulties the Defence is facing with access to the archives. A very practical solution has been suggested, and it appears to be working at the moment. The Prosecution asks to reserve its position until those negotiations are finalised, and if and when the Defence has to file a motion, we will speak to the Defence about the documents on our list and whether or not they would -- whether or not the Defence will object to the tender of any of the ECMM documents. We'll speak to them out of court and we'll speak to them and work out whether there may be an acceptable method agreeable to both parties of us providing them to the Trial Chamber in advance. But the Prosecution isn't in a position to address any of those issues in any detail at the moment, but we will do so in the future, when the matter is further advanced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber expects the motion to be filed by next week. It will be dealing with the whole problem and it will also suggest specific approach, the Defence approach, with regard to the documents. We are going to rise for the day, due to the lack of witnesses, and we shall convene again on Monday afternoon. Unless you want to say something else, but be brief, please, because normally we should have had a break already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Very quickly. At the Pre-Trial Conference, we submitted to you a list of documents, which is still missing, according to our records, documents that should be provided to us by the Prosecution. We've had talks already with the Prosecution about it. Yesterday we were given additional documents. But we think that there's still some missing documents. Allow me to inform you as to this. Two very quick examples: Next week, we're going to have witnesses who will testify to the events that occurred in the town of Miletici. In this respect, there are two exhibits which we deem important, and they are in the pre-trial brief PT44 and PT608. They're still missing in the list of exhibits to be provided by the Prosecution. In order to avoid any undue delay in the proceedings next week, we would like the said documents to be researched so as to see whether we can have them. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you properly, you're going to meet with the Prosecution to handle this issue, and we had said this earlier on, of course: If there were exhibits mentioned and referred to in the indictment, of course the Defence should have them. There should be no problem for you to receive them. I believe. This being so, we shall convene again on Monday afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of December, 2003.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.50 a.m.
